$doc: The securaCV hub's first-boot provisioning plan: the ordered steps that turn stock Home Assistant OS into a working hub. Generated so the on-device installer, the docs, and the flasher UI can't disagree about the sequence. Every step states why it exists and what it buys, because a user watching software configure their home should be able to answer 'what is this doing, and why?' at every line.
order_matters: Repositories before installs (nothing installs from an unregistered repo); broker before the things that publish to it; Frigate's config before Frigate starts, or it crash-loops with nothing to do.
slug_note: Each add-on step carries both `addon` (the friendly slug, for display) and `supervisor_slug` (what the Supervisor REST API answers to). They differ for third-party add-ons: a repo add-on is addressed as `<repo_hash>_<slug>`, so securaCV's `privacy_witness_kernel` becomes `d0491a67_privacy_witness_kernel`. Install by the supervisor_slug or the API returns 'add-on not found'.

repositories.why: Frigate is a third-party add-on: Home Assistant can't see it until its store repository is registered. Installing Frigate before this step is what fails with 'add-on not found'.
The securaCV add-on lives in this project's own repository, added the same way.

steps.title: Register the add-on repositories
steps.what: Tell Home Assistant where the Frigate and securaCV add-ons come from.
steps.why: Home Assistant only installs add-ons from repositories it knows about. Both of ours are third-party, so nothing else in this plan can work until they're registered. The Supervisor API does this unattended; the `ha` command line cannot, which is why the by-hand path makes you click through the store UI.
steps.for_what: Makes the next two installs possible.

steps.title: Install the Mosquitto broker
steps.why: MQTT is the shared language of the hub: cameras' detections and each Canary's events all arrive as MQTT messages, and Home Assistant discovers new sensors the same way. The broker is the post office they all hand messages to — nothing downstream can talk without it, which is why it goes first.
steps.for_what: The message bus every other piece publishes to and reads from.

steps.title: Install Frigate (the camera eyes)
steps.why: Frigate is what actually looks at camera video and decides 'that's a person'. securaCV deliberately does NOT re-implement detection — it subscribes to Frigate's events over MQTT and turns them into signed, identity-stripped claims. So Frigate is the eyes; securaCV is the witness that writes down what was seen.
steps.for_what: Turns camera video into detection events on the broker.

steps.title: Write Frigate's configuration
steps.what: Copy the curated config to `/addon_configs/ccab4aaf_frigate/config.yml`, then start Frigate.
steps.why: A stock Frigate knows nothing about your hub. This config points it at the Mosquitto broker (so securaCV hears its detections), tracks the same objects the witness kernel labels, and — importantly — leaves recordings AND snapshots OFF: securaCV is 'claims, not recordings', so nothing stores raw imagery unless you deliberately turn it on. It also uses a distinct MQTT client id, so a second detector (say a Jetson) can join without the two knocking each other offline.
steps.for_what: Makes Frigate talk to your hub instead of sitting idle.
steps.dest_note: The Frigate add-on reads config.yml from its OWN add-on config directory — NOT /config/frigate.yml. Editing the wrong file is the classic 'I changed it and nothing happened'.
steps.user_must_finish: Add your camera's RTSP URL and set `enabled: true` on it — the shipped example camera is disabled so the config is valid before you've added anything. Frigate ignores a disabled camera silently, so this is the one edit nobody can make for you.

steps.title: Install the securaCV witness kernel
steps.what: Install the `privacy_witness_kernel` add-on, set it to Frigate mode, and start it.
steps.why: This is the part that makes the system a witness rather than a camera system. It subscribes to Frigate's detections, strips identity, and writes each one into a signed, hash-chained log that can be verified later without trusting us. We set it to `frigate` mode BEFORE starting: its factory default is `standalone`, which only serves a setup wizard, so without this the 'unattended' install would quietly stop short of ever producing a claim. In frigate mode it auto-discovers the broker installed above (no MQTT to type) and generates + persists your device signing key automatically — open the add-on panel afterwards to back that key up, because losing it means you can't verify your own log.
steps.for_what: Turns detections into tamper-evident, privacy-preserving claims.

user_supplied.what: Your camera's RTSP URL, and `enabled: true` on that camera.
user_supplied.why: Camera addresses and credentials are yours; we can't guess them, and we won't scan your network to find out. This is the one step that is genuinely manual.
